faq.q: What is the difference between margin and markup?
faq.a: Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price. Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. A 50% markup equals a 33.3% margin.

faq.q: How is the loan payment calculated?

faq.q: What does break-even mean?
faq.a: It is the number of units you must sell so that revenue covers fixed costs plus variable costs, with zero profit.

faq.q: What is the difference between margin and markup?
faq.a: Margin is profit divided by the selling price. Markup is profit divided by cost. A product that costs $40 and sells for $65 has a 38.46% margin and a 62.5% markup.

faq.q: How do I price for a target margin?
faq.a: Divide the cost by (1 minus the margin). For a 40% margin on a $40 cost: $40 ÷ 0.60 = $66.67.

faq.q: How is break-even calculated?
faq.a: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit), rounded up to a whole unit. Add a profit goal to fixed costs to find the units needed to reach it.

faq.q: How do I calculate sales tax?
faq.a: Multiply the taxable amount by the rate. At 8.25%, tax on $100.00 is $100.00 × 0.0825 = $8.25, so the total is $108.25.

faq.q: How do I take sales tax out of a total (reverse sales tax)?
faq.a: Divide the total by 1 plus the rate. For a $108.25 total at 8.25%: $108.25 ÷ 1.0825 = $100.00 before tax, so the tax was $8.25.

faq.q: Which states have no sales tax?
faq.a: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon have no statewide sales tax. Alaska lets local governments charge one, averaging about 1.82%.

faq.q: Are these the exact rates for my city?
faq.a: No. The state rate is exact, but the local figure is a population-weighted average from the Tax Foundation (as of July 1, 2026). Local rates vary by city, county and district, so use "My exact rate" with the rate from your receipt or state revenue department when you need to be precise.

faq.q: Where do the rates come from?
faq.a: State and average local rates come from the Tax Foundation, "2026 Sales Tax Rates, Midyear Update" (rates as of July 1, 2026). Tax rules on what is taxable (food, clothing, services) also differ by state.
